name: Amira Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a contract logistics warehouse, which means we store and ship stock for lots of different brands. One aisle is face creams, the next is vitamins, then dog food. I push a cart with a handheld scanner, pick the orders, and drop them at packing. Day shift, seven till three, plus Saturdays when I can get them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the variety, and I like seeing which products sell, because it helps my side business. What wears me out is the contracts. When a brand leaves us, half the shift loses hours overnight, and that's happened twice since I started. My shift manager, Paolo, also says I chat too much at the packing bench, which is fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's a useful tool, not a miracle. I'd keep using it, because I already do every day. I'd probably post something like, still using it, still picking boxes, nothing changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's okay. My warehouse wage pays the rent, and my little makeup reselling business pays for everything else. I buy clearance stock and sell it online, and AI writes my listings. If nothing big changes, I just keep growing that slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the warehouse job and put more evenings into the reselling, maybe aiming for two hundred extra a month. I'd keep about five months of bills saved, which I have now, and not touch it. I'd also start a free online course on bookkeeping so I know what I'm doing with the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, actually. Calm. It's my plan without any surprises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about those contracts leaving? Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It did the first time, I lost about a third of my hours for six weeks. Now I keep the savings partly for that. And the reselling helps fill the gap when hours drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you live with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My flatmate Leila, we've shared for four years. She works in a call centre, so she's the one who should worry about AI, honestly. I keep telling her to learn the tools.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful tool**, not a miracle.
I'd post that I'm **still picking boxes** and still using it daily.
think: My **warehouse wage** pays the rent, and reselling pays the rest.
A plateau lets me **grow the side business** slowly.
do: Put more evenings into reselling, aiming for **two hundred** extra a month.
Keep **five months** saved and take a free **bookkeeping** course.
feel: **Calm**, because her plan runs without surprises.
S0.quote: My warehouse wage pays the rent, and my little makeup reselling business pays for everything else.
fieldNote: She already **plans for shocks** like brands leaving and hours dropping.
Her **side business** is real and uses AI every day.
She worries more for her flatmate Leila's **call centre** job than her own.

steps.text: Grow the online makeup reselling by two hundred a month
Take a free online bookkeeping course
Keep five months of bills untouched in savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should learn the tools now, not wait. I'd say it to Leila and to the girls at packing, and I'd post a few tips online. I'm the annoying one who sends everyone AI shortcuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly upside. If AI writes my product listings in ten seconds, I can run five times as many listings from my bedroom. The warehouse would get slowly more robots, but slowly is fine, I'd be building something on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd scale the reselling, maybe rent a storage unit by the end of the year. I'd ask Paolo if I can help test any new scanning or AI picking system at work, because I'd rather be the one who knows it. I'd move a bit of my savings into stock for the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A bit worried for Leila, but excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planners upstairs who do the wave schedules. That's exactly what AI does well. And the customer service team for our brands, they'd shrink fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting savings into stock is a risk. How much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a month's worth of bills, not more. I'd keep four months as a safety net. I've lost money on a bad batch of lip gloss before, so I've learned.

say: I'd tell everyone to **learn the tools** now.
I'd post **AI tips** online and send shortcuts to colleagues.
think: AI writing listings lets me **run five times** as many products.
Slow robot spread in the warehouse gives me **time to build** on the side.
do: Scale reselling and rent a **storage unit** by year end.
Ask Paolo to let me **test new AI picking** systems.
Move **one month** of savings into stock.
feel: **Excited**, with some worry for her flatmate Leila.

fieldNote: Steady Disruption looks like an **opportunity** to her.

steps.text: Rent a storage unit for reselling stock by year end

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say everyone needs to move fast, and the government needs some kind of safety net while they do. I'd post a lot about practical tips. At work I'd tell people to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 the AI can run a whole online shop: find stock, write listings, answer buyers. When AI can run a whole online shop by itself, my little side business stops being special overnight. Then by 2031 robots do the picking too, so both my incomes get hit within three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pull back from the reselling and stop buying stock, and get my savings back up to six months. I'd look for jobs that need a person in the room, maybe in the care side or as a beauty therapist, since I know the products. I'd start a course in the first year while I still have the warehouse wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's the first time my plan B doesn't look like a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why beauty therapy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people want a human hand on their face, I think. I know the brands inside out from the warehouse and the reselling. It's a gamble, but it's a gamble on people, not screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said both incomes. How long could you last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With six months saved and Leila sharing rent, maybe eight months of not panicking. After that I'd be asking my parents for help, which I really don't want to do.

say: I'd call for a **safety net** while people retrain fast.
I'd post **practical tips** and tell colleagues to save.
think: By 2028 AI runs **whole online shops**, so my side business loses its edge.
Robots take picking by **2031**, hitting **both incomes** within three years.
do: **Stop buying stock** and rebuild savings to six months.
Start a **beauty therapy** course while still earning in the warehouse.
feel: **Anxious**, because her plan B no longer looks like a plan.
S2.quote: When AI can run a whole online shop by itself, my little side business stops being special overnight.
fieldNote: Fast AGI hits her **side business** before her warehouse job.
She looks for **people-facing** work like beauty therapy.
Asking her **parents** for money is the last thing she wants.

steps.text: Stop buying resale stock and close slow listings
Rebuild savings to six months of bills
Start a beauty therapy course at evening college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good push to get serious. I'd tell people to pick a skill and start. Online I'd share what I'm trying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough time to turn a hobby into a proper business, if I stop treating it like a hobby. The online selling gets squeezed by 2031, so I'd move towards something physical, like a small beauty studio. The warehouse lasts until about 2034, which pays the bills while I build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a beauty therapy course part-time in the first year and keep the reselling running to fund it. I'd use AI to write a business plan and compare studio rents. I'd keep four months of savings and put the rest into training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit nervous, but mostly fired up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the business look like in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small room, maybe in the back of a hairdresser's, doing facials and brows. AI could do my bookings and my social media. I'd be the hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd be afraid of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Failing in front of my family. My dad thinks the warehouse is a good steady job and the rest is a phase. I'd want to prove him wrong.

say: I'd say five years is a **push to get serious**.
I'd share **what I'm trying** online so others can learn.
think: Online selling gets **squeezed by 2031**, so I'd move to physical work.
The warehouse lasts to **about 2034**, paying bills while I build.
do: Start a **part-time beauty course** funded by reselling.

S3.quote: Five years is enough time to turn a hobby into a proper business, if I stop treating it like a hobby.
fieldNote: She uses the **three-year gap** as funding time for a new business.

Proving her **father** wrong is part of the drive.

steps.text: Take a part-time beauty therapy course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's loads of time, so let's not waste it. People should treat it as a ten-year plan. I'd post about it now and then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough to try three different things and fail at two of them. That's actually how I like to work. The warehouse keeps me afloat while I experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, keep everything going and add one new thing, probably the beauty course. Keep reselling with AI, keep saving five months. I'd also put a small amount into an index fund each month, because ten years is long enough for that to grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Ten years feels like freedom more than a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a downside to having that much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You can waste it. I've seen people say they'll start next year for five years running. I'd set myself checkpoints, like a new skill every two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay at the warehouse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Until something else pays more, yes. I like the people and the variety. It's a good base, it's just not my whole life.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my side business and my warehouse job both go within three years. What would help is a safety net while people retrain and cheap short courses for hands-on work, not just computer courses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask how people built their skills. I left school early, so nobody ever handed me a plan. I've always had to build my own, and this is just a bigger one.

headlineQuote: I left school early, so nobody ever handed me a plan. I've always had to build my own, and this is just a bigger one.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old picker** at a contract logistics warehouse who runs a **makeup reselling** side business.
She uses **AI every day** for listings and is pragmatic, not ideological, about change.
She treats the warehouse as a **stable base** while she experiments with new income.
She stays **calm** in slow scenarios but grows **anxious** if fast AGI hits both her incomes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her side business and warehouse job both go within three years.
whatWouldHelp: A **safety net** while retraining and cheap **hands-on courses**, not just computer ones.
